title: The Day a Wave of Molasses Hit Boston #shorts

lines.text: Can molasses kill twenty-one people? In Boston, it did.
On January fifteenth, nineteen nineteen, a tank holding over two million gallons of molasses burst.
A wave of syrup raced down the street at about thirty-five miles an hour.
Twenty-one people died, and about a hundred and fifty were hurt.
The company blamed anarchists. But a court ruled the tank was simply unsound.
Firefighters hosed it with salt water, and the North End smelled sweet for years.
So, can molasses kill? In Boston, it did, and the city never tasted the same.

facts.date: January 15, 1919, about 1 p.m., Commercial Street, North End, Boston (Britannica, Boston.gov)
facts.tank: more than 2 million gallons released (Britannica says up to 2.5M capacity; Boston.gov: wave volume 2.3M)
facts.legal: USIA blamed anarchists; 1925 court-appointed auditor found the tank unsound / owners negligent (Britannica, Boston.gov)
facts.cleanup: salt water sprayed by fireboat Engine 31 broke up molasses (Boston.gov); city smelled of molasses for years (Britannica)
